title: Chrome for researchers on Mac in 2026: tab groups, shortcuts, and Lazur
metaTitle: Chrome for Researchers on Mac: Tab Groups, Memory and Shortcuts

blocks.text: What Chrome for researchers on Mac means in practice

Most researchers do not need a special browser. They need Chrome to hold many sources at once and stay responsive while they read and write. Chrome for researchers on Mac is the same Chrome, set up for the way you work.

Chrome has no research mode that I could confirm. Google's documentation does not list research templates either. So the setup is something you build from features Chrome already has. Google's Chrome page lists tab groups, vertical tabs, split view, Energy Saver, Memory Saver, profile sync for bookmarks and passwords, Google Lens, and extensions from the Chrome Web Store.

This page shows how to use those pieces for literature reviews, grant drafts, and reading lists. It also covers the points where Chrome on a Mac catches people out. Where a detail is unconfirmed, the page says so.
Why open tabs become the real problem

Research in Chrome usually means a lot of tabs. A paper, a dataset page, a Google Scholar results list, a funder's guidelines page, and a co-author's shared document can all sit open at once. Each one feels too important to close.

A Carnegie Mellon study presented at ACM CHI 2021 looked at this habit. It surveyed people about tab management through surveys and interviews. More than half of participants felt they could not close any of their tabs. Thirty percent said they had a tab-hoarding problem.
These figures come from ScienceAlert's coverage of the study. The ACM paper itself did not open for me, so the counts are secondhand. Use them as a sign of the problem, not as a precise measure.
The useful takeaway is not to close fewer tabs. Most people find closing hard. The better goal is to organize tabs so you can ignore most of them until you need them. Tab groups do that job well.
Chrome tab groups for research: one group per question

A tab group is a labeled set of tabs. It collapses into a single header, so the tab strip stays readable. Make one group for each question you are working on. Name it after the question, not after one paper. Paper titles change when you revise. Questions tend to stay put.

To make a group, right-click a tab and look for the option to add it to a new group. The exact label changes between Chrome versions, so read the menu you actually see. Name the group, pick a color, then drag more tabs into it.
A small example helps. Suppose you are writing a methods section, a grant, and a literature summary in the same week. Keep a group for each part of that work.

items: Methods: the sampling paper, the protocol, and the dataset page.
Funder: the call for proposals, the guidelines PDF, and last year's award list.
Reading: papers you have not opened yet, collapsed until you need them.

blocks.text: Collapse and expand a group from the keyboard. Select the group header, then press Space or Enter. Use Control with the left or right arrow to move a tab or a whole group. These keys come from Google's shortcut page.

There is one gap. Google's shortcut page does not list a key combination to create a tab group. Use the mouse or trackpad for that step. Keep the keyboard for moving and collapsing groups after they exist.
Split view and vertical tabs for comparing sources

Split view puts two tabs side by side in one window. Google's Chrome page lists split view for two tabs. Use it when a PDF sits on one side and your notes sit on the other. You can also keep a dataset page next to the table you are copying from.

Vertical tabs move the tab strip to the side of the window. Titles are easier to read there, especially long ones. Google lists vertical tabs on its Chrome page too. Look for the setting in Chrome's settings, then use vertical tabs for a week before you decide to keep them.

blocks.title: Pin the draft tab
blocks.text: Pin the tab for the document you write in. Memory Saver may not put a pinned tab to sleep, so the draft stays ready when you come back to it.
Memory Saver on Mac: what it does and what it skips

Memory Saver puts tabs you are not using into a low-memory state. That frees memory for the tabs you do use. Chrome offers three levels: Moderate, Balanced (recommended), and Maximum. Start with Balanced. Move to Maximum only if the Mac still feels slow under your normal load.

Know the exceptions before a deadline. Memory Saver may not deactivate a tab that has audio or video playing, a screen share, an active download, or a partly filled form. Pinned tabs and tabs with a connected USB or Bluetooth device are on the list too.

blocks.caption: Tab states from Chrome's Memory Saver and Energy Saver help page

blocks.text: The partly filled form matters most for grant work. A half-written application should stay awake, and Memory Saver may leave it alone. A tab you have finished with is a good candidate for sleep. Let Chrome handle that one.

The Mac label is different too. On a Mac, the toggle that shows memory use is called Show memory usage on tab hover preview card. On Windows, Linux, and Chromebook it reads Show tab memory usage. If a guide uses the second name, you will not find it under that name on your Mac.
Energy Saver is a separate feature. It turns on automatically when the Mac is unplugged or the battery is low. It does not turn on while the Mac is plugged in. It can change how games and video run.
You can turn Energy Saver off for the current session. Click the Energy Saver icon in the address bar. That is the fastest fix when a video stutters on battery.

blocks.title: Check before you blame the page
blocks.text: A long reading session on battery can trigger Energy Saver. If a video or a live chart stutters, check the Energy Saver icon in the address bar before you blame the website.
Chrome profiles for research and grant work

A profile keeps its own bookmarks, history, and signed-in accounts. Use one profile for personal browsing. Use another for grant or thesis work. Keep the funder portal and your institutional email in the work profile.

Open the profile menu with ⌘⇧M. Google's shortcut page lists it as the profile or people menu. Switch from there. Chrome can also sync bookmarks and passwords across devices, as Google's Chrome page notes. Turn sync on for the work profile only if you trust that account and that Mac.

The most common mistake is signing into a personal account inside the work profile. Then personal history and saved logins mix with your research records. Check which profile is active before you start a session.
Chrome keyboard shortcuts on Mac for research
Shortcuts speed up the reading loop. The table lists the ones Google documents for Chrome on Mac. Start with new tabs, tab switching, and reopening a closed tab. Add the others as you need them.

rows: Useful after you close a source by mistake
Hold Command and Option, then press Right Arrow
Collapse or expand a tab group
blocks.caption: Shortcuts from Google's Chrome keyboard shortcuts help page

blocks.text: Test each shortcut once on your own Mac. Keyboard layouts and macOS settings can change what a key does. A shortcut that works on a friend's Mac may behave differently on yours.
Accessibility settings that change the keyboard in Chrome

Google's shortcut page makes two points you should know. The tab-group menu requires VoiceOver to be turned on. Some navigation needs Full Keyboard Access enabled on the Mac. The page does not say which shortcuts depend on Full Keyboard Access, so test your common ones.

To look for Full Keyboard Access, open System Settings and go to Keyboard. Look for the keyboard navigation option there. Menu names change between macOS releases, so search System Settings for Full Keyboard Access if you cannot find it.
If you do not normally use VoiceOver, expect the tab-group menu to be a rough edge. Plan your workflow around it. Do not rely on it for a deadline day.
Chrome extensions for saving citations and sources

Chrome extensions come from the Chrome Web Store. Researchers often add a reference manager, a note tool, or a PDF reader. Many reference managers publish their own browser connector. Check the reference manager's own site for the current connector, then install from that link.

Read the permissions before you click Add to Chrome. An extension that can read every page you visit can see your sources, your drafts, and your logins. Install only what you need for the question in front of you.
Keep the list short. Each extension adds work to the browser. Remove the ones you tried and did not use. Check the list again every month.
Keep Chrome current and check your macOS version
Start by checking your version. Open Chrome > About Google Chrome. I could not confirm the current stable number as of November 6, 2026. Treat the numbers below as clues, not final answers.

Google's enterprise release notes list Chrome 152 with a stable date of September 1, 2026. Chrome Platform Status shows Chrome 158 scheduled for stable on November 17, 2026, and currently on Beta. That points to Chrome 157 as the current stable. Confirm it on the Chrome Releases blog before you rely on it.

Support depends on your Mac. For new installs of Chrome 151 and later, macOS 13 or later is required. Chrome 151 removes support for macOS 12. Check Apple menu > About This Mac for your macOS version.
The Chrome Releases blog listed an early stable update for desktop dated November 4, 2026. Updates arrive often, so check the version again after a few weeks.
Mistakes researchers make in Chrome on Mac

items: Naming tab groups after paper titles. Name them after the question instead.
Keeping every tab open so nothing is lost. Save the link in your reference manager, then close the tab.
Assuming Memory Saver will sleep a half-filled form. It may not.
Mixing personal sign-ins into the work profile. Keep the two apart from the first day.
Installing an extension from a copy of a listing rather than the publisher's own page.
Trusting a shortcut list from a random blog. Check Google's page first.

blocks.text: A worked afternoon of literature review in Chrome

Here is a realistic sequence for one afternoon. You are reviewing methods for a grant section. Several candidate papers are already open from earlier. You want to finish a first pass before you write anything.

items: Press ⌘⇧M to open the profile menu, then pick the work profile for this grant.
Right-click a tab and add the methods papers to a new group. Name the group after the question.
Start split view with one paper on one side and your notes document on the other.
Ask Lazur to explain a table that confuses you. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask in plain words.
Hold fn and dictate your first-pass notes straight into the document.
Collapse the group with Space or Enter when the first pass is done.

blocks.text: At the end you can see the question, the sources, and the notes at the same time. Tomorrow you open the group and start where you stopped. The browser did the organizing, and you did the thinking.
Where Lazur fits in a research session
Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

Use explain when you need meaning. Use point when you cannot find a control, since Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Use guide when the steps matter more than the answer. Lazur waits for each click before it moves on.

Use dictate and draft when the words are the work. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. Ask Lazur to draft an email from what is on screen, then read it before you send it. Lazur types text. You decide what goes out.

Use research for background work. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. The run happens in those tabs, not in the ones you have open.
What Lazur will not do in Chrome

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It will not click the Memory Saver setting, move your tab groups, or fill in a grant form. Use it to understand the page, find the control, and draft the words. Keep the clicking with you.
Dictate notes and draft text while you read
Dictation is part of Lazur, and it works in any app. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans. See the [pricing page](/pricing) for the plans.

Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots help with the repeated parts of research writing. Put your standard citation sentence into a snippet. Put an author's unusual name into the dictionary, so it comes out spelled right.
Privacy and memory on a shared Mac
Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did, on the Mac. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
If the Mac is shared with a lab partner, lock the screen when you step away. Press ⌃⌘Q to lock a Mac. Keep your grant work in the work profile, so the next person sees less of it.
What to do next

items: Check your version under Chrome > About Google Chrome.
Make one tab group for the question you are working on now.
Set Memory Saver to Balanced and watch the Mac for a week.
Create a separate profile for grant work and switch with ⌘⇧M.
Read Google's shortcut page once, so the table above is not your only source.

faq.question: Does Chrome have a research mode for Mac?
faq.answer: Not one I could confirm. Google's Chrome page lists tab groups, vertical tabs, split view, Memory Saver, Energy Saver, profiles, and extensions. A research setup comes from combining those features. I did not find Chrome-native research templates in Google's documentation.

faq.question: Which Chrome version is current for Mac right now?
faq.answer: I could not confirm it. Google's enterprise notes list Chrome 152 for September 1, 2026. Chrome Platform Status shows Chrome 158 scheduled for stable on November 17, 2026. So Chrome 157 is probably current. Check Chrome > About Google Chrome for the number on your Mac.

faq.question: How much memory does Memory Saver free up?
faq.answer: Google's help page does not give a figure. It describes three settings and the kinds of tabs it may leave awake. Test it on your own work. Watch memory use in Activity Monitor while you switch between your usual tabs.

faq.question: Will Chrome put my grant application tab to sleep?
faq.answer: It may not. Memory Saver may not deactivate a tab with a partly filled form. Keep the form tab active while you type, and save drafts often. Do not depend on any sleep setting to protect unsaved text.

faq.question: Can I use tab groups without VoiceOver?
faq.answer: Google's shortcut page says the tab-group menu requires VoiceOver. To be safe, create groups with the mouse or trackpad and test your own workflow before a deadline. Keyboard moves and collapses work once the groups exist.

faq.question: Does Lazur work in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes, Lazur works on the screen in any app while you hold ⌥⌘. It explains, points, guides you one click at a time, and drafts text. It does not click for you. Its research runs in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for macOS on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available now.

faq.question: Is my research content used to train AI?
faq.answer: Lazur says content is never used to train AI models. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did on the Mac.
